title: Growing asparagus
subtitle: A perennial bed that takes three years to establish and then crops for twenty
excerpt: Asparagus is a long-term investment: crowns planted in spring produce no pickable spears for two years while the bed establishes, but a well-managed asparagus bed crops for 20 years or more. The brief season in April and May produces some of the finest eating in the kitchen garden.
sourceNotes: RHS asparagus growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on asparagus production, public domain. Mrs Loudon, The Lady's Country Companion (1845), Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dormant bare-root asparagus plant, consisting of a central bud cluster and a spread of fleshy roots. Crowns are planted in spring at 1 year old. Two-year-old crowns are sometimes sold as giving a one-year head start, but they are harder to transplant successfully and the result is usually the same as starting with one-year crowns. The crown is never disturbed once planted; asparagus beds are permanent.

The feathery foliage that develops from asparagus spears that are left to grow unpicked. After the harvest season ends, all remaining spears are allowed to fern up and photosynthesize through summer and autumn; this process builds the energy reserves in the crowns that produce next year's crop. Cutting the fern too early weakens the bed.

content.text: in spring of year one. Pick nothing in year two. Pick sparingly for two to three weeks in year three. From year four onwards, harvest for eight weeks each April and May and the bed will reward you for 20 years. The key rule: let the spears
after each harvest season; cutting them early shortens the productive life of the bed.

Choose a permanent, sunny, open position with well-drained, deep soil. Asparagus is one of the few vegetables that tolerates slightly sandy, lighter soils well; heavy clay is a problem unless improved with grit and compost. The bed must be completely free of perennial weeds before planting; once the crowns are in, deep cultivation is impossible. Dig out every bindweed root, couch grass rhizome, and dock taproot.

Plant in March or April when the soil is workable. Dig a trench 30 cm wide and 20 cm deep. Build a central ridge of well-rotted compost. Drape the crowns over the ridge with the roots spreading on either side, spaced 40 cm apart. The bud cluster should sit 10 cm below the soil surface. Fill in gently, firming without pressure on the roots. Space rows 1 m apart; asparagus needs light and air.

Year one: let all the spears fern up; do not harvest. Keep the bed weed-free; hand-weed carefully around the crowns. Year two: still resist harvesting, or take just one or two spears per plant. Keep ferning. Cut the browned fern down to 5 cm from the ground in late November or February; no earlier, as the fern continues feeding the roots until the frost kills it.

Cut spears when they are 15 to 18 cm tall, using an asparagus knife or sharp knife, cutting 2.5 cm below soil level. Year three: cut for two to three weeks in April and May, then stop. Year four and beyond: cut for up to eight weeks. When the spears become thin and spindly, the season is over; allow them all to fern up from that point.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main asparagus problems in UK growing.

items.symptom: Yellowing, dying fern in summer before autumn
items.cause: Asparagus beetle damage or Fusarium crown rot.
items.fix: Check the stems for black-and-yellow beetles; hand-pick and destroy. If the crown feels soft and the roots have rotted, dig and destroy the affected crowns; there is no treatment for Fusarium.

items.symptom: Bed produces fewer and thinner spears each year
items.cause: Harvesting too heavily, cutting fern too early, or perennial weeds competing with the crowns.
items.fix: Shorten the harvest period. Cut the fern no earlier than November. Hand-weed persistently around the crowns in summer.
